# 10 Strategies to Reduce GenAI Costs

Michelle Meng | Product Marketing Director for GenAI | September 29, 2026

Token volume also compounds across orchestration. An AI application may make several model or tool calls before it produces a final response, so teams should measure the full request path.
- ### GPU and accelerated computing

Graphics processing units (GPUs) and other accelerators account for a substantial share of costs when organizations host or fine-tune models. A project’s economics are determined by the amount of useful inference or training work that capacity produces.

Poor concurrency or oversized instances can leave accelerator capacity underused and raise the cost per request. Teams running dedicated capacity should monitor utilization and throughput together, so performance targets don’t hide waste.

...

### 3. Improve GPU utilization

Dedicated accelerators become expensive when demand is uneven or capacity remains idle. Teams that operate GPU-backed inference can compare provisioned capacity with actual throughput throughout the day and identify whether memory, request scheduling, batch size, or application design is limiting useful work.

Where the workload permits, use batching and concurrency to increase throughput, right-size accelerator configurations, and adjust capacity as traffic changes. For workloads with irregular demand, a consumption-based managed service can help reduce the financial penalty associated with continuously reserved but unused hardware.

...

### 10. Evaluate AI infrastructure based on total price-performance

Compare infrastructure using the economics of the complete workload. Include the costs of model serving, data management, operations, and idle capacity when evaluating a workload.

Deployment options have different cost curves. For example, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Enterprise AI offers on-demand and dedicated serving modes. On-demand serving suits workloads that don’t require reserved capacity, while dedicated AI clusters provide dedicated GPU capacity for hosting and fine-tuning. OCI Enterprise AI serving modes integrate factors such as unit price, workload shape, and utilization into price-performance evaluations.

...

OCI provides several ways to match AI resources to workload requirements. Opportunities to reduce costs come from combining model choice, serving capacity, network and data architecture, and financial controls rather than optimizing one component in isolation. OCI offers the following cost-management capabilities:

- ### Use high performance AI infrastructure efficiently

OCI’s AI infrastructure includes bare metal and virtual machine GPU options, along with cluster networking designed for GPU workloads. Enterprises can choose infrastructure according to model size, throughput, latency, and training or inference needs instead of assigning the same compute profile to every AI workload.

Cost control still depends on utilization. Measure dedicated GPU capacity against actual throughput and demand so idle resources are easy to spot.
- ### Choose models based on workload requirements

...

- ### Optimize costs across the complete AI stack

OCI billing and cost management tools provide budgeting, cost analysis, forecasting, and anomaly detection. Use cost analysis tools to examine spending by OCI service, compartment, and tag. This analysis helps teams connect AI infrastructure consumption with the applications and organizations responsible for it.

...

Accurate comparisons often use a common unit, such as cost per successful request at the required quality and latency. Include engineering and operational costs rather than comparing only API prices with GPU prices. A hybrid approach can also be economical, and different workloads within the same enterprise may justify different serving models.

...

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure can help enterprises apply GenAI cost management strategies. OCI Enterprise AI provides access to frontier and open-weight models, helping teams match model capability and cost to each workload. On-demand capacity and dedicated AI clusters help teams align serving resources with workload demand, while the underlying OCI AI infrastructure is designed to deliver high performance at a low cost. OCI cost governance and budgeting tools give businesses a unified view of AI spending, helping them identify cost drivers across AI applications and continuously improve economics. Together, these capabilities support efforts to reduce AI costs and improve workload economics.

...

How does GPU utilization affect AI costs? 

Low GPU utilization raises the cost of each useful inference or training job because the organization is paying for accelerator capacity that isn’t producing work. Better batching and capacity management can increase useful GPU throughput. Teams should watch latency and application quality at the same time because maximizing raw utilization isn’t useful if it causes service problems.

A language model may charge according to the amount of text it processes, while GPU-based services may charge for time or reserved capacity. Within any cost structure, variables such as retries or agent loops can multiply the underlying usage, so a workload can become more expensive even when the number of business tasks stays flat.

For AI workloads running on OCI, billing and cost management tools provide cloud cost records that can be organized around the resources that support a workload. For example, the cost analysis tool can show spending trends and group cost data by tags or compartments. You can set budgets that trigger alerts against defined spending thresholds, while cost reports add resource-level records for invoice analysis and allocation.

OCI Enterprise AI provides on-demand inference and dedicated AI cluster options for supported models. On-demand mode uses pay-as-you-go inference, while dedicated mode commits to cluster capacity for a defined period. Pairing those cloud cost records with application-level request telemetry helps connect infrastructure spending to the model calls and the completed business work that generated it.

results.title: NVIDIA NeMo Relay now natively supports Oracle Generative AI | ai-data-science
results.author: Federico Kamelhar
highlights:
# NVIDIA NeMo Relay now natively supports Oracle Generative AI

 September 24, 2026 8 minute read 

Federico Kamelhar

Distinguished Engineer, Agentic AI

By Federico Kamelhar, Senior Principal Architect, Agentic AI — Oracle

NVIDIA NeMo Relay, NVIDIA’s open-source library that runs alongside the existing agent harness to observe and control AI agents, now treats Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Generative AI as a first-class provider. Every chat call to the managed service — Meta Llama, Cohere Command, xAI Grok, Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT, or an imported NVIDIA Nemotron 3 model — is recognized, decoded, and normalized by the runtime, across all three of the service’s wire formats, with the same support in Rust, Python, and Node.js.

...

- A complete audit trail, with zero instrumentation. Every model call and tool call becomes a recorded step — request, response, model, tool arguments, token usage — grouped per run and isolated across concurrent agents. When something goes wrong in production, the trajectory is the record you debug against.
- PII redaction that protects your telemetry, not your prompts. Redaction rewrites what is recorded, while the model receives the original. In the runs behind this post, a two-line policy recorded the requester’s email as `j*******@example.com` everywhere in the trace, with the original nowhere in it.
- Guardrails around every call. Relay’s conditional-execution guardrails can block a request before it reaches the model, and its sanitize guardrails can rewrite what gets recorded. In the runs behind this post, a guardrail rejected a request for a production password before OCI Generative AI was ever called — the same guardrail can govern every other provider you route through.
- Cost visibility per step, per run, per provider. Normalized token usage flows through a pricing catalog into the trajectory. The runs in this post landed at fractions of a cent, itemized — including one trace that spanned the managed service and a self-hosted Nemotron, with cost attributed across both.
- Your observability stack, not a new one. Trajectories export as ATIF, OpenTelemetry spans, or OpenInference output.
- Nothing leaves your tenancy. The runtime is an in-process library, not a gateway: your HTTP clients, your OCI signers, your network path.

results.title: Real World Analysis of Ideal AI Workloads for NVIDIA Vera on OCI | cloud-infrastructure
results.author: Sanjay Basu, Calvin Smith, Carson Abernethy
highlights:
# Real World Analysis of Ideal AI Workloads for NVIDIA Vera on OCI

 September 16, 2026 9 minute read 

Sanjay Basu

Senior Director - Gen AI/GPU Cloud Engineering

Calvin Smith

Carson Abernethy

Why AI native teams are asking for NVIDIA Vera to run their workloads on an 88 core agentic Arm CPU

For most of the last decade the interesting question about a data center CPU was how many cores it had and what they cost per hour. That question is now less useful than it looks. The workloads that determine how much an AI system costs to run have moved off the model and onto the layer around it. Orchestration, tool dispatch, sandboxed code execution, retrieval, and the operational plumbing that keeps an agent loop alive are all CPU work, and they are increasingly on the critical path. NVIDIA built Vera for exactly that path, and OCI will be the first cloud to deploy it at hyperscale.

OCI = First Hyperscaler with Vera Sysems Oracle was thrilled to be one of the companies to receive the first Vera CPU Systems back in May of 2026, which were hand delivered by Ian Buck, VP of hyperscale and performance computing at NVIDIA, to OCI, Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX.

...

1. The first is price and performance on the workloads they actually run. These are companies that measure cost per token and cost per completed task across the full stack, not cost per GPU-hour. When the layer around the model is a large and growing share of that cost, a CPU that is purpose-built for that layer changes the economics in a way a faster GPU does not. The memory bandwidth per core in particular gets called out as exceptional, because it maps directly to the concurrent, memory-scattered work these teams are bound by.
2. The second is that OCI is first. OCI will be one of the first cloud providers to deploy Vera at hyperscale, with plans to deploy hundreds of thousands of units beginning this year. For a company whose product depends on agentic infrastructure, being able to run production agentic AI on Vera before that capacity is broadly available elsewhere is a real advantage, not a marketing point.
3. The third is deployment flexibility. On OCI, Vera will be available as both bare metal and virtual instances, which suits the CPU nature of the offering and lets teams start small and grow. The teams we are working with are talking about starting with a handful of racks and scaling from there as the workloads prove out, and OCI’s model supports exactly that shape of adoption.

...

The independent testing so far ran on pre-production silicon in an open chassis, , so per-watt and per-dollar comparisons are not yet possible from public data. Real production thermal and power behavior will only be visible once the platform ships. The standalone Vera comparison against the parts it competes with most directly in the Arm category have not been run in public yet. OCI’s own benchmark work is aimed at closing exactly those gaps, on the real fabric with realistic data sizes, and we will publish it soon.

results.title: Investigate OCI cost anomalies with Oracle Analytics Cloud Explain – Part 3 of 3 | analytics
results.author: Sandy FADEL, Eugene Simos
highlights:
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) cost and usage data can show an unexpected change before its cause is clear. Oracle Analytics Cloud (OAC) Explain helps you explore a selected measure, such as Total Cost, against the attributes in the available dataset. It surfaces notable segments, drivers, and anomalies that can focus an investigation.

Explain generates hypotheses; it doesn’t prove root cause. Use it to identify the service, region, tag, or time period that merits closer inspection, then validate the result with operational evidence.

...

Start with a curated OAC dataset that contains OCI cost and usage records, a representative history of normal activity, and useful dimensions such as service, region, compartment, tag, and billing period. Confirm that data refreshes have completed before interpreting a recent change. If recent data is incomplete or delayed, investigate the data pipeline first.
